value.overview: The Checker-throated Stipplethroat (Epinecrophylla fulviventris) is a small insect-eating antbird of humid tropical forests in Central America and northwestern South America. It was formerly known as the Checker-throated Antwren or Fulvous-bellied Antwren. This active bird is especially associated with hanging dead leaves, vine tangles, and dense understory vegetation, where it searches for arthropods. It often travels in pairs, family groups, or mixed-species feeding flocks.
value.classification: The species belongs to the antbird family Thamnophilidae and the order Passeriformes. It is one of the stipplethroats in the genus Epinecrophylla.
value.identification: The Checker-throated Stipplethroat is about 10–11 cm long. Adults have a warm fulvous or buff-colored belly, a relatively long plain tail, and contrasting dark-and-white patterning on the throat and upper breast. Males usually show a darker throat marked with pale spots, while females have a paler buff throat and breast. The species is small, active, and often difficult to see as it moves through tangled understory vegetation. Its song is a series of sharp, repeated, somewhat accelerating notes.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges from southeastern Honduras through Nicaragua and Costa Rica to western Panama, and from Panama south through western Colombia and western Ecuador. In Costa Rica it is a resident of humid forest, especially on the Caribbean slope and in suitable foothill areas, with records also from protected forests near San José. It occupies evergreen lowland and foothill forest, mature secondary woodland, forest edges, and dense vine tangles. In Costa Rica it generally occurs from the lowlands to about 900 m elevation.
value.migrationStatus: Year-round resident, including in Costa Rica; it is not known to undertake regular long-distance migration.
value.breeding: Breeding information varies geographically. In Costa Rica, nesting has been reported mainly from March through August. The nest is a deep pouch made from plant fibers, rootlets, fungal material, and dead leaves, lined with finer fibers and suspended from the end fork of a thin twig. It is usually placed below 2 m in a sapling, though higher nests have been recorded. The clutch normally contains two marked eggs. Both parents incubate and feed the young.
value.dietFeeding: The diet consists mainly of arthropods, including cockroaches, crickets, katydids, spiders, and other insects. It searches methodically through vine tangles, hanging dead leaves, moss, epiphytes, and leafy branches, often extracting prey from debris caught in the vegetation. Foraging usually takes place in the understory and lower mid-story. The species commonly feeds in pairs or small family groups and regularly joins mixed-species feeding flocks; it only occasionally follows army-ant swarms.
value.behavior: This is an active, relatively inconspicuous understory bird that usually remains within dense vegetation. Pairs and family groups maintain territories and may participate in mixed-species flocks. During territorial encounters, males can display from nearby perches by lowering the head, puffing the plumage, swaying, and calling continuously. Its sharp, repeated vocalizations help reveal its presence when visual observation is difficult. The species is strongly associated with dead-leaf and vine-tangle microhabitats while moving through forest vegetation.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population size has not been quantified and is thought to be decreasing, but the species has a large range and is considered reasonably common in much of it.
